items.quote: The most High created this Fift Essence as the root of life in Nature
items.note: The Fift Essence is named as one thing, made by God as the root of life, for the preservation of the four qualities of the human body.

items.quote: The celestiall Fire that burneth not, is the soul and life of all Creatures
items.note: A fire that does not burn is said to be the soul and life of all creatures; it is set beside the Fift Essence as the same subject.

items.quote: the Influences of all celestiall bodies which are communicated to the sublunary to every one in particular, these are concentred in this one
items.note: All heavenly influences, spread to each thing below the Moon, are said to be gathered into this one subject.

items.quote: The Theater of the secrets of all Natur's Light
items.what: The Theater of the secrets of all Natur's Light
items.note: First of a long run of titles given to the one subject; it is called a theater of nature's secrets.

items.quote: the Glasse of God's Mysteries, and the Miracle of universall Nature; the Fift Essence of the whole frame of the world, and the whole world Regenerated
items.what: the Glasse of God's Mysteries; the Miracle of universall Nature; the whole world Regenerated
items.note: Further titles for the same subject: a glass of God's mysteries and the whole world regenerated.

items.quote: the Son of the Sun and Moon, who by his ascending into Heaven and descending into the Earth hath obtained all power of superior and inferior things
items.note: The subject is spoken of as a person, a son of Sun and Moon who ascends and descends; the figure points beyond a plain description of a substance.
items.term: Son of the Sun and Moon

items.quote: the Habitation of all metallick, minerall, and vegetable Forms, which God created under the Globe of the Moon
items.what: the Habitation of all metallick, minerall, and vegetable Forms
items.note: The subject is said to house the forms of metals, minerals and plants below the Moon.

items.quote: it is truly the spirit of Life which pierceth through all other spirits
items.note: The subject is said to be the spirit of life, passing through all other spirits.

items.quote: is altogether one and the same with the spirit of our body, the bond between the Body and Soul
items.note: Croll holds this spirit to be the same as the spirit of the human body, binding body and soul together.

items.quote: there is need of the Balsom of life as a means to be sought from Externalls, by which the internall is restored
items.note: The inner life is to be restored by a balsom of life taken from outside things.

items.quote: without which fuell it goeth out of the body as a flame from the lamp-wick for want of oyle
items.note: Life is pictured as a flame that goes out without this fuel.

items.quote: it is the most simple Matter which the Best and Greatest Lord generated out of the spirit of this world for the restauration and preservation of Humane Nature
items.note: The subject is called a most simple matter, made by God out of the spirit of this world.

items.quote: which hath been altogether unknown to the Physitians of our time
items.note: This matter is said to have been wholly unknown to the physicians of Croll's time.

items.quote: it never came into their Schools who goe not into the Temple of Apollo through the right door, but break through the Roofe
items.note: The physicians of the schools are said to enter knowledge wrongly, not by the right door; a figure of illegitimate access.

items.quote: while they hold the keys of Sciences in unrighteous captivity, they bring to passe nothing with their decrees, and ordinances
items.note: These physicians are charged with holding the keys of knowledge captive and achieving nothing.

items.quote: others who desire to enter in a right way they hinder in their laudable course by their pernicious dehortations
items.note: They are charged with keeping others from the right way by dissuading them.

items.quote: The life of natural things is the Union of the Ideall Light, as also with the Ideall of Heaven and Earth.
items.note: The margin note defines the life of natural things as a union with an ideal light.

items.quote: in this Stone the universal Nature of things shineth forth
items.note: Beside the titles of the subject, the margin note calls it a Stone and an Art.

items.quote: The Tincture is the Fife Essence of the Microcosm
items.note: The margin note equates the Tincture with the fifth essence of the Microcosm.

items.quote: the first and most perfect Being and that Cabalisticall unary number
items.note: The Tincture is said to come very near the first being and a cabalistic number one; a turn toward a sense beyond the medical.

items.quote: Paracelsus calleth it the perfect, perpetuall,
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The margin note gives Paracelsus' names for it: a perfect, perpetual balsom of physicians or philosophers.

items.quote: the Defensive of old age, the Universall medicament, which like the invisible Fire consumeth all diseases
items.what: the Defensive of old age, the Universall medicament
items.note: Further names, in the margin note, for the same balsom.

items.quote: Those Ancients who had most perfect knowledge of Things have called this Fist Essence the middle nature of Soules.
items.name: Ancients
items.note: The margin note reports that the Ancients called the Fift Essence the middle nature of souls.

items.quote: the true originall of all corporall diseases, in the judgement of the best Physitians, is the enormity of the Naturall proportion of the Three First
items.note: The cause of bodily disease is put in the disorder of the proportion of the Three First.

items.quote: as common Physitians say, the disorder and ill disposition of the four Elements or Humors
items.name: common Physitians
items.note: The common physicians' way of naming the same cause, by four elements or humors, is set beside Croll's Three First.

items.quote: this foresaid Medicine, which is in it selfe the matter of our Creation may be congeneous and uniform to the substance, consisting in equality
items.note: The Medicine is said to be the matter of our creation and of one kind with the body's substance.

items.quote: the Fift Essence or Fift Virtue resulting from the purer Essence of the four Elements, purified, incorruptible is compared to Heaven
items.note: The Fift Essence, also called Fift Virtue, is said to come from the purer essence of the four elements.

items.quote: nor doth it admit any malignant spirit, but they all fly from it
items.note: No malignant spirit can stay near this essence.

items.quote: it expelleth as much as is possible by Nature all accidentall corruptibility from which any sicknesse or weaknesse may arise
items.note: Because it hardly corrupts, it drives out corruptibility that causes sickness, within the limits of nature.

items.quote: by reconciliation cureth againe the diseases that hapned by the exaltation of the Three Principles
items.note: Diseases come from the exaltation of the Three Principles and are cured by reconciling them; the same paragraph calls them the Three First.

items.quote: When the purified Elements are reduced to a pure and equall simplicity then is got the Medicine that prolongeth life
items.note: The margin note describes the medicine as got by bringing purified elements to an equal simplicity.

items.quote: the inequality and dominion of one over another is it that breedeth diseases
items.note: The margin note puts disease in one element ruling over another.

items.quote: Mans health consisteth in the agreement and union of the Three First Substances
items.note: Health is the agreement of the Three First Substances.

items.quote: when they are exalted and set on fire by the Stars, the intestine wars follow
items.note: The Stars are said to inflame the three substances and cause inner war, that is, disease.

items.quote: they give place to the Essence of Fire which consumeth the disease and separateth the pure from the impure
items.note: The Essence of Fire consumes the disease and separates pure from impure.

items.quote: Health consisteth in a Temperate body.
items.note: The margin note puts health in temperance of the body.

items.quote: Let it not seem strange to any that the sole act of one Thing should be variously diversified, not as to it selfe
items.note: One thing's single act works differently according to what receives it.

items.quote: as the celestiall Sun hardneth the Clay and softneth the Wax
items.note: The margin note's example: the sun hardens clay and softens wax.

items.quote: that Fift Essence of the Human Body bindeth the Elements or Humors in Peace and Harmonicall league
items.note: The Fift Essence keeps the elements or humors in peace.

items.quote: reduceth to the true Temperament by making equall the unequall, and strengthneth the naturall heat and substantificall moysture
items.note: It restores temperament by equalising and strengthens natural heat and moisture.

items.quote: the Radicall Humor, the Vitall Balsom and most precious Nectar of our Life
items.note: The Radicall Humor is named also the Vitall Balsom and Nectar of life.

items.quote: the strengthning power of the Human body and of Animalls proceedeth from the spirit of Life
items.note: The body's strength comes from the spirit of life.

items.quote: keep the predisposed or fore-qualified Man safe and sound from sicknesse, with the comelinesse of youth
items.note: The essence is said to keep a suitably prepared man healthy and youthful.

items.quote: even to his Naturall death, that is to that Terme of Life which the Omnipotent God hath appointed to Man for disobedience
items.note: Natural death is defined as the term of life God appointed for disobedience; the medicine works only up to it.

items.quote: such a man who shall use it prudently and seasonably with a devout calling upon the Name of the Lord
items.note: Its use is tied to prudence, right timing and prayer, and to a body not extremely weakened.

items.quote: the True Fonntaine of Physick, the Conservation of Life, the Restitution of health, the Renovation of lost youth
items.note: The spiritual medicine is named the true fountain of physic and the renewal of lost youth.

items.quote: which hath the Nature and Heat of Heaven (not of our mortall and corruptible)
items.note: Its heat is heavenly, not mortal heat.

items.quote: this true Triacle of Phylosophers, which like the Elixir of life is the superlative and last consolation of Mans body
items.note: Another name for the medicine, compared to the Elixir of life.

items.quote: For in every kind there is a certaine One that holdeth the first degree in that kind
items.note: Croll argues that each kind has one first member; this medicine is first among medicines.

items.quote: this Medicine is made of the more incorruptible and efficacious Matter that can be under Heaven, that is, the Soule or Spirit of the world
items.note: The matter of the medicine is named the Soule or Spirit of the world.

items.quote: the Man that useth it with the moderation of other meat, may live as long as the ancient Fathers
items.note: Used moderately like food, it is said to give a life as long as the ancient Fathers'.

items.quote: The Heat of the Sun and Moon is that Naturall Heat whereby every thing is digested
items.note: The margin note equates the heat of Sun and Moon with natural heat; CH6.56 uses the same words of our own natural heat.

items.quote: The Spirit is the life and Balsom of all Naturall things.
items.note: The margin note calls the Spirit the life and balsom of natural things.

items.quote: From those two fountaines the SUN and MOON, as Suchtenius learnedly discourseth, springeth the Naturall and Vitall Spirit of the world
items.name: Suchtenius
items.note: Suchtenius is cited for the teaching that the spirit of the world springs from Sun and Moon.

items.quote: there can be nothing in all the world that may or can be without a spark of this Spirit
items.note: Every thing holds a spark of this spirit; it carries every occult quality into lower bodies.

items.quote: This Celestiall Spirit which is one and the same with our Naturall spirit
items.note: The heavenly spirit is said to be the same as our natural spirit, and to be our natural heat.

items.quote: It digesteth the nourishment that Man taketh, and breeds good blood in all the members
items.note: The spirit, as natural heat, digests food and makes good blood.

items.quote: if it be hindered by sicknesse that it cannot so well doe its office, the nourishment is not well concocted
items.note: Hindered by sickness, the spirit digests badly, breeding bad blood and weakening the heart's spirit.

items.quote: a full extinction, consumption and dissipation of that spirit, which is the Naturall Death
items.note: Natural death is defined here as the full dissipation of the spirit, after old age.

items.quote: that spirit and Naturall Heat in Humane bodies so weakned and hindred must be increased and strengthned
items.note: The task set: to increase and strengthen the weakened spirit and heat, to delay its dissipation.

items.quote: The Life of Man is the Astral Balsom. the Balsamick Impression, the Celestiall and Invisible Fire, the Aire shut up, and the Tincturing Spirit of Salt.
items.note: The margin note gives a run of names for the life of man.

items.quote: every agent when it begins to act, doth not move toward any thing below it selfe, but to that which is equall like and sutable to it
items.note: Principle: an agent acts toward its like.

items.quote: this strengthning also must be by its like, that is, by that Celestiall Heat of the Sun and Moon, and the other Planets
items.note: The spirit is to be strengthened by its like, the heavenly heat of Sun, Moon and planets.

items.quote: or with those things in which the Virtue of the SUN and MOON is most potent and doth most abound, or is lesse restrain'd by matter
items.note: Or by things in which the virtue of Sun and Moon is strongest; these things are not named here.

items.quote: the spirit or that supernall Fire is got out of them by art
items.note: The spirit or supernal fire is drawn out of such things by art; the art is not described here.

items.quote: But burning Heat, consuming all things, and darknesse, making all things barren, are proper to the Elementall and Inferior Fire.
items.note: Elemental fire is defined by burning and barrenness, against the heavenly heat that makes fruitful.

items.quote: The Celestiall or that Spirit of the world and the Naturall Spirit of our body is one and the same Spirit
items.note: The margin note repeats that the world's spirit and our natural spirit are one.

items.quote: That same (Heat) therefore is excluded, as also with it all divers and contrary things, such as are all the inferior Elements.
items.note: Elemental heat and the inferior elements are excluded from the medicine.

items.quote: so far as they are yet drowned in a thick grosse matter, and as yet not separate from it
items.note: Things still sunk in gross matter, not separated from it, are subject to corruption.

items.quote: Medicines ought to be preserving and very durable, and remote from corruption
items.note: A medicine must itself be lasting, or it would corrupt rather than preserve.

items.quote: tis but in vaine to think to preserve a corruptible body by a putrid and corruptible thing
items.note: A corruptible remedy cannot preserve a corruptible body.

items.quote: Every corruptible weak and feeble thing added to its like, augmenteth it
items.note: Like added to like increases it, so corruptibility is increased.

items.quote: too many Physitians of our time who labor in vaine to cure Men of their maladies by their grosse and corporall compositions of Medicines
items.note: Physicians of the time are faulted for gross bodily compounds.

items.quote: but a higher speculation is here required
items.note: The text says a higher understanding is needed here, turning from bodily remedies.

items.quote: For whereas diseases are not corporall, but spirituall and lurking in the spirits, they also call for spirituall medicines.
items.note: Diseases are spiritual and need spiritual medicines.

items.quote: One Like added to its like maketh it more Like.
items.note: The margin note states the principle of like added to like.

items.quote: The vitall spirit in Man & the Elemental is one spirit.
items.note: The margin note makes man's vital spirit one with the Elemental, while the text sets elemental heat apart and excludes it.

items.quote: that vitall spirit (which is the Radicall Moysture and Heat
items.note: The vital spirit is said to be the radical moisture and heat.

items.quote: the innate Mummy, and hath its seat in the midst of Mans heart, as the sustentacle of all our life
items.note: The vital spirit is also named the innate Mummy, seated in the heart.

items.quote: they must seek after not the Elementall, but that Celestiall Heat of the Sun and Moon that dwelleth in the more incorruptible substance that is to be found under the Globe of the Moon
items.note: The heavenly heat is to be sought in the most incorruptible substance below the Moon; the lines given do not name that substance.

items.quote: when it is prepared and made up into a medicine and most pleasant meat, so that being taken by the mouth
items.note: It is prepared into a medicine and pleasant food, taken by mouth.

items.quote: it may presently pierce and passe throughout the human body, keep every thing incorrupt
items.note: Taken, it passes through the whole body and keeps it from corruption.

items.quote: strengthen, inflame and augment the weak Naturall Heat or Fire
items.note: Its effect: to strengthen the weak natural heat.

items.quote: This is the duty of a true Physitian, and of the more sound Phylosopher.
items.note: This work is named the duty of the true physician and philosopher.

items.quote: The Innate Heat and Radical Moysture of the Microcosm are sustained by the MacrocoMacrocosmicall Heat and Moysture of the Sun and Moon
items.note: The margin note: the body's heat and moisture are sustained by those of Sun and Moon.

items.quote: For thus he might preserve our body from corruption, retard old age, keep youth flourishing in its vigour to the very poynt of death
items.note: The physician might so keep the body young until death.

items.quote: were it not for the wages of sin, withstand death
items.note: Only sin's wages keep him from withstanding death itself.

items.quote: The Tincture doth so cleanse the Balsom, that our children in the tenth generation may see the effect of it living so long, Paracels.
items.name: Paracels.
items.note: The margin note gives Paracelsus' claim that the Tincture cleanses the Balsom for ten generations.

items.quote: Paracelsus calleth it the Element of FIRE, which like the Sun of the Terrene or inferiour Firmament may be the greatest Secret for the removing all diseases
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: Paracelsus' name for it, the Element of FIRE, called the greatest secret against disease.

items.quote: may be the greatest Secret for the removing all diseases
items.note: The Element of FIRE is called a secret.

items.quote: that Essentiall Fire worketh in the body, as the Flame and Nettle doth without the body
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The essential fire works inside the body as flame and nettle work outside it.

items.quote: that of right he may here be vindicated from the unjust calumny wherewith he was branded
items.note: Croll sets out to defend Paracelsus against slander.

items.quote: the Balsamick Mummy, the Vitall Body, the liquor of Life, the Native or Radicall Humor which the Spirit of Life moveth or acteth
items.what: the Balsom of Nature, the Balsamick Mummy, the Vitall Body, the liquor of Life
items.note: Croll's account of Paracelsus' meaning lists several names for one thing to be restored and preserved.

items.quote: to the last gasp of Life without any sicknesse, paine and griefe
items.note: Paracelsus' aim is given as health up to the last breath, not escape from death.

items.quote: being Poysoned in his body by his malicious and inhuman adversaries
items.note: Croll states that Paracelsus was poisoned by his adversaries.

items.quote: for he came to the Naturall Terme of his Life by an untimely and violent death of a draught of Poyson
items.note: A death by poison is called the natural term of his life, while elsewhere natural death is the slow dissipation of the spirit or the term God appointed.

items.quote: many maliciously scoffe in their strange fictions, that he by this his medicine would presumptously prepare himselfe an entrance and way to the immortall health of his body
items.name: many
items.note: The scoffers' claim, reported to be rejected: that Paracelsus sought bodily immortality.

items.quote: The Humors of life do nourish the spirit of life.
items.note: The margin note: the humors of life feed the spirit of life.

items.quote: See Paracel. in the sift Tome among his Physicall fragments, sol. 162.
items.name: Paracel.
items.note: The margin note sends the reader to a writing of Paracelsus beside this passage.

items.quote: Cease therefore henceforth to blame Paracelsus in that he promisedlong life to others, but scarce came to full age himselfe.
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The margin note answers the charge that Paracelsus promised long life yet died young.

items.quote: GOD is the Centre of all Creatures, by how much the more any draw near to him, by so much the more blessed
items.note: God is the centre; nearness to him brings blessedness and constancy.

items.quote: that Centre or One, to wit, the immutable will of God
items.note: The Centre or One is defined as God's unchanging will.

items.quote: Blessednesse is in unity, not in the circumference; in Christ, not in the world, is Peace and the Rest of Soules.
items.note: Blessedness lies in unity and in Christ, not in the many things of the world.

items.quote: He that continueth united with God in Christ doth like God and the Angels never wax old.
items.note: The margin note: union with God keeps one from growing old.

items.quote: who exclaime that this interpretation is forced and far setch'd
items.note: The margin note calls the reading of long life as union with God an interpretation, which critics call forced; it marks a second sense of long life.

items.quote: In vaine will those husks & scraps of Paracelsus rise up that use to do
items.name: husks & scraps of Paracelsus
items.note: Critics, called husks and scraps of Paracelsus, are reported in order to be rejected.

items.quote: shall forget all Things and leave sensible and Temporall things behind him
items.note: Leaving sensible things and being united to the one Centre makes one grow young rather than old.

items.quote: And this is the true Long Life of the Cabalists, and of Paracelsus
items.note: The true Long Life is defined as union with the Centre, God.

items.quote: he waxeth young rather than old
items.note: Growing young is used of the soul's union with God, a second sense beside the bodily youth of CH6.54 and CH6.55.

items.quote: which he so often and so earnestly begg'd for by Prayer and holy hope in his Hymns and Soliloquies
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: Paracelsus' Hymns and Soliloquies are cited as asking for this long life.

items.quote: the true Enochean Life
items.note: The long life is named the Enochean Life.

items.quote: And this is the true Long Life of the Cabalists, and of Paracelsus
items.note: Here true long life is union with God; in CH6.55 the medicine gives bodily life as long as the ancient Fathers'.

items.quote: he that is not united to this most united Fountain-like and only Unity by adhaesion, must of necessity perish for ever
items.note: Whoever is not united to the Unity perishes for ever.

items.quote: be separated from the Light and Life by the second death
items.note: The fate of the un-united is named the second death.

items.quote: the utter Darknesse of the Caliginous world, which deprivation and want of the sight of God is the most bitter of all punishments
items.note: The dark world is defined as want of the sight of God.

items.quote: To know GOD himselfe the maker of all things, and passe into him with a full image of his likenesse
items.note: To know God and pass into him is named the true and solid philosophy.

items.quote: whereby thou mayest be transform'd, and made (as it were) a God
items.note: The text marks its own words with as it were: being made a God is not meant plainly.

items.quote: this at last will prove the True and sollid Phylosophy
items.note: The true philosophy is named and set apart.

items.quote: The MIND therefore of Adept Phylosophers
items.note: The Adept Philosophers and their mind are named as the subject of what follows.

items.quote: to whom one is All in all, and All are one in One
items.note: For the adepts, one is all and all is one.

items.quote: look upon these transitory things with the left eye, but on Heaven with the right
items.note: A figure of two eyes for two ways of seeing.

items.quote: Phil. 3.20.
items.name: Phil.
items.note: The margin note cites a writing beside the words on conversation in Heaven.

items.quote: The Mystery of Divine Matrimony with Man.
items.what: The Mystery of Divine Matrimony with Man
items.note: The margin note names a mystery of divine marriage with man.

items.quote: of these Adept Phylosophers hath ever been far off and estranged from the Cavill above mentioned
items.note: Points back to the cavil already mentioned, the scoffers' charge in CH6.62.

items.quote: raised up out of the sepulchre of their body or out of the dead Works of Darknesse
items.note: The body is called a sepulchre; rising from it is used of meditation.

items.quote: they could open the Eyes of their Heart, and be turned to God in the Sabbath of their Heart
items.note: Eyes and Sabbath of the heart: inward senses of outward words.

items.quote: one simple (intuitive vision or) sight from within, a kind of an Essentiall touch of the Divinity
items.note: The Blessed Spectacle is defined as a simple inward sight, an essential touch of the Divinity.

items.quote: which beauty is incomprehensible to the Old Creature
items.note: The beauty of the Chiefest Good cannot be grasped by the Old Creature.

items.quote: the most beautifull Nothing (that is, the shadow and region of Darknesse and Death)
items.note: The text glosses its own term: the beautiful Nothing is the region of darkness and death.

items.quote: returned to the BEING of BEINGS (from whom we are wandred)
items.note: The goal is return to the Being of Beings.

items.quote: they leave themselves, and totally go out from themselves contemning all things corporeall and incorporeall
items.note: The adepts go out of themselves, despising all things.

items.quote: the most wise Hermes and most pious Phylosopher of reverend antiquity the Antesignan of Naturall Phylosophers and first Prophet
items.name: Hermes
items.note: Hermes is cited as acknowledging, in his Monade, the sacred silence of this knowledge.

items.quote: doth also acknowledge in his Monade
items.name: Monade
items.note: A writing of Hermes is named as the place of his acknowledgement.

items.quote: is a sacred, Heavenly, and hid silence, the quiet or Rest of the sences and all things
items.note: The knowledge and contemplation of the One is called a hid silence.

items.quote: after an unutterable manner, shall be altogether but one thing, in one MIND which is above every MIND
items.note: The final union of minds happens in a manner that cannot be uttered.

items.quote: It is the intimate vision of GOD, and the Intuitive knowledge of GOD, which also hapneth by the Light of Grace to the separate Soul even in this world
items.note: This union is defined as the intimate vision of God, possible even in this life.

items.quote: many holy men by vertue of the Deifick Spirit have tasted the First fruits of the Resurrection in this life
items.note: Holy men have had a foretaste of resurrection in this life.

items.quote: that spirituall Death of the Saints (which the Jewes call the kisse of Death)
items.name: Jewes
items.note: The Jewes' name for the spiritual death of the saints: the kiss of Death.

items.quote: if the fulnesse of Life may be called death
items.note: The text says death is here used of the fullness of life, not plainly.

items.quote: We must die to the World, Flesh, Blood, and the whole Animall Man
items.note: Croll's demand: to die to world, flesh and the animal man.

items.quote: who would faine have got into those Inmost secrets, and entred into Paradise by the excesse or going out of the MIND
items.note: The inmost secrets are entered only by going out of the mind.

items.quote: the Man that liveth in nothing but the Mind, is as an Angel
items.note: One who lives only in the mind is like an angel.

items.quote: not after the Limus Terrae the Eearthy Mind
items.note: Limus Terrae is glossed as the earthy mind.

items.quote: into the Sea of Nihilitude or Nothingnesse
items.note: Nihilitude is glossed as nothingness, into which the friends of God cast themselves.

items.quote: By the Soul abiding and standing stedfast, embracing its Image of Divinity or MIND united to GOD by Christ, we enjoy actuall Blessednesse.
items.note: Actual blessedness comes by the soul holding to its divine image, the MIND, united to God by Christ.

items.quote: By the access of this beam, ray, or celestiall Stone all drosse is purified, and the darknesse of ignorance is driven away.
items.note: Beside the adepts' mind, the margin note calls a beam or ray a celestial Stone that purifies dross and ignorance; Stone used of the mind's light.

items.name: Eccl.; Psal.; Rom.
items.note: Writings cited in the margin beside this passage.

items.quote: Whatsoever is not God, is Nothing, and ought to be esteemed as nothing.
items.note: The margin note defines Nothing as all that is not God.

items.quote: INFORTUNIUM.
items.note: A Latin word set in the margin beside the word for unhappiness in the text.

items.quote: Lactantias mentioneth Hermes not so much among the Naturall Phylosophers, as among the Sybylis and Prophets, as the true Orpheus.
items.name: Lactantias
items.note: Lactantias is cited as placing Hermes among prophets.

items.quote: Lactantias mentioneth Hermes not so much among the Naturall Phylosophers
items.note: The text calls Hermes the leader of natural philosophers; the margin note's source puts him less among them than among the prophets. The text also calls him first Prophet.

items.quote: All things are seen and lookt into with one presentiall glance.
items.note: The margin note: in this vision all things are seen in one glance.

items.name: Exod.; Es.; 2 Cor.; Psal.
items.note: Writings cited in the margin beside the spiritual death of the saints.
